name: Zond 2
short_status: Crippled hours after launch on 30 November 1964 by a jammed solar panel, on about half power, it fired the first electric thrusters beyond Earth orbit, went silent by May 1965 and passed Mars unheard on 6 August 1965.
tagline: OKB-1 (USSR) · Soviet Union · Flyby · 1964 · The first attempts Failure
stats: plasma thrusters, the first electric propulsion beyond Earth orbit
of design power after one solar panel jammed
reported miss distance at Mars on 6 Aug 1965, and disputed

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 30 November 1964 from Site 1 at NIIP-5 (Baikonur) on a four-stage Molniya 8K78, vehicle G15000-29. Sources give the time as 13:12 UTC (NSSDCA and Siddiqi) or 13:25 UTC (McDowell's GCAT); we could not resolve the 13-minute difference.

facts.label: Designation
facts.value: 3MV-4A No. 2. The 3MV was the third-generation planetary bus, with 3MV-3 for Mars impact and 3MV-4 for Mars flyby; the A suffix marks a modified test article. Some catalogues drop the A and write 3MV-4 No. 2.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: Published figures disagree badly: 890 kg (NSSDCA, McDowell), 950 kg (LePage), 960 kg (Russian Wikipedia) and 996 kg (Siddiqi). No source we consulted explains the spread.

facts.label: Actual objectives
facts.value: A letter from Leonid Smirnov, chairman of the Military Industrial Commission, to the Central Committee dated 28 November 1964, two days before launch, states the flight was to test 3MV elements and do interplanetary science, and, if the systems worked, to impact Mars and deliver commemorative pennants to the surface.

facts.label: What was announced
facts.value: The TASS communique of 2 December 1964 gave only two goals: shaking down onboard systems in long-duration spaceflight, and scientific research in interplanetary space. Mars was not mentioned.

facts.label: Ascent profile
facts.value: The fourth stage placed the spacecraft in a 153 by 219 km parking orbit and then reignited to inject it toward Mars. The spent Blok I and the settling-motor unit reentered on 1 and 2 December 1964.

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: Radiation detector, charged-particle detector, magnetometer, piezoelectric micrometeoroid detector, radio telescope, cosmic-ray nuclear component experiment, ultraviolet and X-ray solar radiation experiment, and an imaging system. Perminov notes Zond 2's radio suite dropped the 8 cm and metre-wavelength transmitters that Mars 1 carried.

facts.label: Plasma thrusters
facts.value: Six ablative pulsed plasma thrusters designed by A. M. Andrianov at the Institute of Atomic Energy, where Lev Artsimovich led the plasma work. A capacitor bank of about 100 microfarads at roughly 1 kV discharged across coaxial electrodes separated by a fluoroplast (PTFE) insulator, ejecting plasma at up to 16 km/s at temperatures near 30,000 K. They were an alternative actuator for the attitude control system, commandable from the ground in place of the nitrogen jets.

facts.label: Thruster test
facts.value: Total running time is given as 70 minutes. Accounts of the timing differ: NSSDCA says 8 to 18 December 1964, English Wikipedia gives 14 December at 4.2 million km from Earth, and Siddiqi records all six firing twice on 18 December just before communications deteriorated.

facts.label: Solar panel failure
facts.value: One of the two panels did not unfold after separation from Blok L, leaving power at roughly half the expected level. The cause is given as a broken tug cord meant to pull the panel free at separation, or a protective shroud that failed to retract. Firing the plasma engines to shake the spacecraft finally freed it on 15 December 1964, after the date for the first midcourse correction had passed.

facts.label: Secondary failure
facts.value: Russian sources add that the onboard programme timer failed shortly after injection onto the interplanetary trajectory, leaving the spacecraft in poor thermal conditions; weeks of reduced power then took the rest of the onboard systems down.

facts.label: Loss of contact
facts.value: Contested. NSSDCA records a putative, unconfirmed midcourse manoeuvre on 17 February 1965 and loss of contact in early May 1965. A declassified US weekly intelligence review gives 7 April 1965 as the last session. The Russian Academy of Sciences space council says May 1965. Soviet authorities announced the loss publicly on 5 May 1965, and LePage notes communications were already erratic by 18 December 1964.

facts.label: Mars encounter
facts.value: 6 August 1965, a silent uncontrolled pass. The commonly cited miss distance is 1,500 km at a relative speed of 5.62 km/s; some later reconstructions put it near 650,000 km. Nothing was tracking the spacecraft, so both figures come from trajectory propagation and neither was measured.

facts.label: Final orbit
facts.value: Heliocentric, roughly 0.98 by 1.52 astronomical units, inclined about 6.4 degrees to the ecliptic, with a period near 508 days.

facts.label: The Zond name
facts.value: Zond means probe in Russian. It was the label used for 3MV flights announced as engineering tests rather than as Mars or Venera missions, so the destination could be left out of the communique. Zond 1 (Venus, April 1964) and Zond 3 (lunar far side, July 1965) carried the same name.

timeline: Leonid Smirnov's letter to the Central Committee sets out the real objectives: test the 3MV design, do interplanetary science, and impact Mars with pennants if all goes well.
Launch from Site 1 at Baikonur into a 153 by 219 km parking orbit, then injection toward Mars by Blok L. Within hours the first session shows power at about half the expected level.
TASS announces the flight as Zond 2, describing systems testing and interplanetary research and saying nothing about Mars.
The six plasma thrusters are test-fired, the first electric propulsion operated on a spacecraft beyond Earth orbit. Sources place the firings anywhere in this window.
Shaking the spacecraft with the plasma engines finally frees the jammed solar panel. The window for the first midcourse correction has already closed.
All six thrusters are fired twice, according to Siddiqi. Communications with the spacecraft are becoming erratic.
A midcourse correction is reported by some accounts. NSSDCA describes it as putative and unconfirmed.
Date given for the last communication session in a declassified United States weekly intelligence review from 1965.
Soviet authorities publicly announce that contact with Zond 2 has been lost.
NASA's Mariner 4 flies past Mars and returns the first close-up photographs of the surface, three months after Zond 2's last confirmed signal.
Zond 2 passes Mars, silent, at a reported 1,500 km, and continues in solar orbit.

images.caption: A black and white photograph of a 3MV spacecraft on its handling ring against a dark backdrop, showing the ribbed umbrella high gain antenna, the two thermal radiator hemispheres, the perforated panel structure, the magnetometer boom and the latticed descent cone on top. NASA released it captioned as Zond 2; the same photograph appears on mentallandscape.com captioned as Zond 3, and the two vehicles were near identical 3MV craft.
images.credit: NASA on The Commons, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A full scale replica of Zond 3 on display in the Tsiolkovsky State Museum of the History of Cosmonautics in Kaluga, filed on Commons under the category 'Replica of Zond 3'. Zond 3 was a 3MV-4 and Zond 2 a 3MV-4A, and the two vehicles were near identical.
images.credit: Stolbovsky, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; Tsiolkovsky State Museum of the History of Cosmonautics, Kaluga
